title: AI agents in STEM
subtitle: From a convincing answer to checkable scientific evidence
author: Dr Woon Kai Lin

lessons.title: AI, solvers and scientific responsibility
lessons.outcome: Separate fluent explanations, deterministic computation and physical validation.

question.prompt: A deterministic solver returns the same result twice. What can you conclude?

answers.text: Its calculation is repeatable under the same conditions; physical correctness still needs checks.
answers.feedback: Yes. Repeatability is valuable, but boundary conditions, units, numerical accuracy and model validity still need independent checks.

answers.text: The result must represent the real system accurately.
answers.feedback: Repeating a wrong boundary condition repeats the same wrong result. Repeatability does not establish physical accuracy.

answers.text: An AI agent can now approve the result without reviewing inputs.
answers.feedback: A solver cannot decide whether the supplied problem represents the intended system. The scientist remains responsible for inputs and interpretation.

lessons.title: Build a reproducible computing environment
lessons.outcome: Distinguish installation, successful execution and numerical validation.

question.prompt: Gmsh and CalculiX are installed and a test job completes. What should you do next?

answers.text: Check a small reference problem, its units and boundary conditions, and retain versions and outputs.
answers.feedback: Correct. A reproducible reference case checks the numerical workflow beyond successful installation.

answers.text: Treat successful installation as proof that every future simulation is valid.
answers.feedback: Installation only establishes software availability. Each model still has assumptions and discretization errors.

answers.text: Delete the input files because the completion message is sufficient evidence.
answers.feedback: A completion message cannot reconstruct the problem. Keep the inputs, versions and numerical outputs needed for review.

lessons.title: Tools, skills and checked agent workflows
lessons.outcome: Explain how tool access, reusable instructions and solver evidence play different roles.

question.prompt: An agent has MCP tool access and a SKILL.md file. Which evidence supports accepting its numerical result?

answers.text: Inspectable inputs and solver outputs checked against the stated requirements and a reference case.
answers.feedback: Yes. Tool access enables actions and a skill guides the method; evidence and verification support the result.

answers.text: The existence of the skill file proves the physics is correct.
answers.feedback: Instructions can be incomplete or applied incorrectly. A skill file is a method, not a numerical validation result.

answers.text: A fluent explanation is enough even if the solver was never run.
answers.feedback: A persuasive explanation is not an observed computation. Check that the claimed action actually ran and inspect its outputs.

lessons.title: Working code can still contain wrong physics
lessons.outcome: Audit material properties, units and model scope independently of syntax.

question.prompt: A script runs without errors but its elastic modulus uses the wrong units. What is the appropriate response?

answers.text: Correct the units and rerun the model, then compare with an independent physical or analytical check.
answers.feedback: Correct. Syntax success does not repair incorrect physical quantities; the corrected model needs a fresh check.

answers.text: Keep the result because the program exited successfully.
answers.feedback: An exit code tests execution, not the physical meaning of the numbers.

answers.text: Relabel the plotted units without changing the calculation.
answers.feedback: Changing a label does not correct the material parameter used by the solver. Repair the input and regenerate the result.

lessons.title: ORCA: access, method and supporting evidence
lessons.outcome: Design a reusable computational chemistry workflow with explicit assumptions and checks.

question.prompt: Which addition makes a reusable ORCA skill scientifically useful?

answers.text: Explicit charge, multiplicity, method and basis choices, convergence checks, and preserved inputs and outputs.
answers.feedback: Yes. The electronic state and numerical settings define the calculation; inspect convergence and retain evidence.

answers.text: A tool connection alone, with default settings left unexamined.
answers.feedback: Access does not specify the electronic state or establish a suitable method. Defaults need justification for the system.

answers.text: Only a final energy number, with all intermediate evidence removed.
answers.feedback: An isolated energy number omits the geometry, state, method and convergence evidence needed to interpret or reproduce it.

lessons.title: ORCA demonstration: verify before saving the skill
lessons.outcome: Distinguish scheduling status from a completed and checked ORCA result.

question.prompt: SLURM returns a job ID for an ORCA calculation. What does that establish?

answers.text: The scheduler accepted the submission; completion and scientific checks still need evidence.
answers.feedback: Correct. Inspect job completion, ORCA normal termination, convergence and the relevant numerical results.

answers.text: The geometry is a verified minimum.
answers.feedback: A submission ID says nothing about optimization convergence or vibrational stability. A minimum requires suitable further checks.

answers.text: The energy is accurate for the intended scientific question.
answers.feedback: Scheduling status cannot validate the chosen electronic structure method or its accuracy.

lessons.title: Circuit design with measurable acceptance criteria
lessons.outcome: Separate AI coordination, ngspice circuit analysis and KiCad board checks.

question.prompt: An amplifier meets the requested low-frequency gain. Is that enough to accept it?

answers.text: No. Check the bandwidth and the other specified operating constraints as well.
answers.feedback: Correct. Acceptance requires all relevant requirements, including bandwidth, operating point and the validity of the model.

answers.text: Yes. A matching gain guarantees the required bandwidth.
answers.feedback: Gain and bandwidth are separate requirements. A circuit may match one while failing the other.

answers.text: Yes, if the schematic looks professionally drawn.
answers.feedback: Diagram quality is not performance evidence. Use the netlist, model and measured or simulated response.

lessons.title: Circuit demonstration: a failed requirement is evidence
lessons.outcome: Interpret an AC response and retain the failure rather than changing the requirement.

question.prompt: A small-signal model has about 10× gain but a cutoff near 100 kHz against a 150 kHz minimum. What is the result?

answers.text: The design fails the bandwidth requirement, even though its low-frequency gain is acceptable.
answers.feedback: Correct. About 100 kHz is below the 150 kHz minimum. Preserve the failure and revise the design or model with justification.

answers.text: It passes because the low-frequency gain is about 10×.
answers.feedback: Meeting gain does not compensate for failing the stated minimum bandwidth.

answers.text: It passes if the horizontal axis is relabelled in MHz.
answers.feedback: A unit conversion does not change the physical cutoff or the acceptance threshold.

lessons.title: Match the model to the physics
lessons.outcome: Separate a lost monitoring connection from simulation failure and request evidence about the current job state.

question.prompt: The monitoring connection to an HPC simulation drops. What can you conclude?

answers.text: The current state is unknown; retain the last verified progress and inspect scheduler and simulation outputs.
answers.feedback: Correct. A lost monitoring connection limits what is known about the current job; it does not establish a physical or numerical failure.

answers.text: The molecular system is definitely unstable.
answers.feedback: A connection failure is an operational observation. Molecular instability requires evidence from the trajectory and simulator outputs.

answers.text: The simulation has definitely completed successfully.
answers.feedback: A lost connection cannot confirm completion. Obtain a current scheduler status and inspect the expected output files.

lessons.title: Bilayer case study: define the observable
lessons.outcome: Distinguish local water contacts, deep-water occupancy and uncertainty in a defined analysis region.

question.prompt: A low mean local water-contact count is reported. What follows from that mean alone?

answers.text: It does not establish zero penetration; inspect the defined region, distribution, sampling and uncertainty.
answers.feedback: Correct. A small mean can include intermittent or spatially localized occupancy. Local contacts and deep-water counts describe different subsets.

answers.text: Water never enters any part of the bilayer.
answers.feedback: A nonzero or rounded low mean is not a universal zero-event claim. Check the event definition and full distribution.

answers.text: Local contacts and deep-water occupancy are interchangeable observables.
answers.feedback: They count different subsets defined by geometry and distance criteria. Keep the definitions separate.
